title: Does Organic Farming Grow Less Food?
question: Does organic farming really grow less food?
alternates: How Much Less Does an Organic Field Produce?
premise: The weight of evidence says organic yields less, by less than often claimed. Ponisio and colleagues pooled 1,071 comparisons from 115 studies in 38 countries and found organic yields 19.2% lower (95% credible interval 15.5 to 22.9%), with conventional ahead for every crop type, a smaller gap than earlier meta-analyses, and they note publication bias may overstate it. A 2017 review adds that organic yields are typically limited by nitrogen. The dissent is a one-sentence summary in the American Academy of Pediatrics abstract that well-designed studies show comparable yields, not a yield analysis of its own.
whyWatch: Whether organic can feed the world turns on one number, how much less an organic field yields. A meta-analysis of more than a thousand comparisons puts a figure on it, and explains why some reports call the yields comparable.
tension: A pediatric clinical report says well-designed studies show organic yields comparable to conventional; a meta-analysis of 115 studies across 38 countries finds a consistent gap for every crop type.

arc.hook: Same crop, same region, one field organic: how much less comes off it?
arc.conflict: The studies do not agree, and both sides have a case.
arc.evidence: Lay the studies side by side (Crowder and Reganold 2015 meta-analysis, organic farm profitability, Ponisio 2015 meta-analysis, organic yield gap, Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming, AAP 2012 clinical report on organic foods, abstract): design, sample, what was measured.
arc.resolution: About a fifth less on average, consistently across crops; the comparable-yield claim rests on a single summary sentence, not on the pooled data.
arc.takeaway: The conditions under which the claim holds, instead of a yes or no.

central.text: Studies disagree on whether organic farming yields less food per acre than conventional farming

claims.text: Organic farming yields less food per acre than conventional farming

guess.note: Meta-analyses put average organic yields roughly a fifth lower, with large variation by crop and management.

questions.question: Does organic farming really grow less food?

central.text: Studies disagree on whether organic farming yields less food per acre than conventional farming

questions.premise: The weight of evidence says organic yields less, by less than often claimed. Ponisio and colleagues pooled 1,071 comparisons from 115 studies in 38 countries and found organic yields 19.2% lower (95% credible interval 15.5 to 22.9%), with conventional ahead for every crop type, a smaller gap than earlier meta-analyses, and they note publication bias may overstate it. A 2017 review adds that organic yields are typically limited by nitrogen. The dissent is a one-sentence summary in the American Academy of Pediatrics abstract that well-designed studies show comparable yields, not a yield analysis of its own.
questions.tension: A pediatric clinical report says well-designed studies show organic yields comparable to conventional; a meta-analysis of 115 studies across 38 countries finds a consistent gap for every crop type.
questions.whyWatch: Whether organic can feed the world turns on one number, how much less an organic field yields. A meta-analysis of more than a thousand comparisons puts a figure on it, and explains why some reports call the yields comparable.

arc.hook: Same crop, same region, one field organic: how much less comes off it?
arc.conflict: The studies do not agree, and both sides have a case.
arc.evidence: Lay the studies side by side (Crowder and Reganold 2015 meta-analysis, organic farm profitability, Ponisio 2015 meta-analysis, organic yield gap, Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming, AAP 2012 clinical report on organic foods, abstract): design, sample, what was measured.
arc.resolution: About a fifth less on average, consistently across crops; the comparable-yield claim rests on a single summary sentence, not on the pooled data.
arc.takeaway: The conditions under which the claim holds, instead of a yes or no.

questions.question: Is organic farming actually better for the planet?

central.text: Organic farming needs more land to produce the same amount of food

questions.premise: Not clearly, per unit of food. In Clark and Tilman's meta-analysis of paired life-cycle studies, mostly from high-input farming in Europe and North America, organic systems needed 25 to 110% more land, used 15% less energy, had 37% higher eutrophication potential and similar greenhouse gas emissions, because manure releases nitrous oxide that offsets the savings from skipping synthetic fertiliser. The authors say this does not make conventional farming more sustainable, since they could not measure pesticide and other impacts, and organic may have benefits outside their data. What dwarfs both is the food itself: ruminant meat has 20 to 100 times the impacts of plant foods, while the two systems differ by tens of percent.
questions.tension: Organic avoids synthetic fertiliser and most synthetic pesticides, so it must be greener; but it needs more land for the same harvest. A meta-analysis of life-cycle studies finds both effects, and the authors refuse to call either system more sustainable.
questions.whyWatch: Many people buy organic for the environment. Measured per kilogram of food, organic wins on some impacts and loses on others, and the choice of food turns out to matter far more than the label.

arc.hook: Per field, organic looks greener; per kilogram of food, the picture changes.
arc.conflict: The claims pulling in different directions: "Organic food costs substantially more than conventional food"; "Organic food is worth its price premium for health reasons"; "Organic farming yields less food per acre than conventional farming"; "Organic farming needs more land to produce the same amount of food"; "Organic and conventional farming have similar greenhouse gas emissions per kilogram of food"; "Organic farming is better for the environment than conventional farming"; "What you eat matters more for your food's carbon footprint than whether it is organic".
arc.evidence: Each claim's verdict, strongest study first.
arc.resolution: Organic trades less energy and fewer synthetic inputs for more land and more nutrient runoff, with similar emissions; for the planet, what you eat matters far more than whether it is organic.
arc.takeaway: A decision rule the viewer can apply.
